name: Oats / rice-and-chicken carbs for bulking

lead: A standard bulk built on oats, rice and chicken means eating above maintenance calories with inexpensive carbohydrate and lean-protein staples to add muscle and build a bigger physique.

The chain is a calorie surplus supplying fuel for hard training, with adequate protein supporting muscle growth alongside resistance training. Wikipedia reports a well-established link between positive energy balance and muscle growth; the specific foods have not been trialled as a set.

paras: Lifters eat large portions of oats at breakfast and rice with chicken at other meals, raising portions to stay in surplus, and favour slower-digesting carbohydrates. Bulks typically run for months, with muscle added gradually.
Larger surpluses and longer bulks add more body fat, and some lifters report needing a harder cut afterward.

angle.text: Lifters build a bulk around oats, rice and chicken to eat in a calorie surplus affordably and add muscle for a bigger physique. Cheap carbs supply fuel for hard training, and a surplus with enough protein supports growth. The link between positive energy balance and muscle gain is well established.

lead: A "standard bulk" built on oats, rice and chicken means eating in a calorie surplus using inexpensive, easy-to-prepare carbohydrate and lean-protein staples so the body has the energy and amino acids to build muscle. The payoff people seek is a larger, fuller physique: more muscle on the frame, which also changes how shoulders, arms and chest look in clothes.

Wikipedia describes bulking as eating above maintenance needs and reports a well-established link between positive energy balance and muscle growth.[1][2] Oats are a calorie-dense grain (about 389 kcal and 17 g of protein per 100 g uncooked), cooked white rice is a compact carbohydrate source (about 130 kcal and 29 g of carbohydrate per 100 g), and chicken breast supplies protein, about 22 g per 100 g raw according to Wikipedia.[3][4][5]

Bodybuilding references note that a larger surplus or a longer bulk adds more body fat, which is why lifters alternate bulking with a cutting phase.[1] No trial has tested oats, rice and chicken as a named bulking diet; the research that exists concerns the general principles of energy surplus and protein, and trials that compare oats with rice for other outcomes.[6][7]
infobox: 389 kcal, 16.9 g protein, 66.3 g carbohydrate, 11.6 g fibre, about 4 g beta-glucan[3]
About 130 kcal, 28.6 g carbohydrate, 2.4 g protein[4]
About 22 g protein and 2 g fat per 100 g[5]
Bodybuilders typically cut for about 12 to 14 weeks before a contest[1]
Clean bulk, dirty bulk, lean bulk

paras: Bodybuilders commonly alternate an off-season bulking phase with a pre-contest cut of roughly 12 to 14 weeks.[1] Clean bulking aims for muscle with limited fat gain, usually moderate carbohydrate, moderate protein and low fat, and it takes longer; dirty bulking uses a large surplus with less tracking, often with foods such as burgers and fries, and tends to add more fat so that a more aggressive cut is needed afterward.[1] Some lifters find the dirty approach psychologically easier because it removes the pressure of strict meal planning.[1]

The oats, rice and chicken pattern sits at the clean end of that range. Foods are inexpensive, shelf-stable or easy to batch cook, and plain enough that portions can be measured and scaled up or down, which is why they recur in bodybuilding meal-prep culture and in lifting forums.[1][8]

Oats are cleaned and dehulled into groats and then processed into steel-cut oats, rolled oats or oat flour, and are mainly eaten as porridge. Uncooked they provide about 389 kcal, 66.3 g carbohydrate including 11.6 g of fibre, 16.9 g protein and 6.9 g fat per 100 g, with about 4 g of soluble beta-glucan.[3] Wikipedia reports that regular oat consumption lowers LDL and total cholesterol, an effect attributed to beta-glucan, and that people with coeliac disease need caution because oat products are often contaminated with wheat and barley.[3] A 2021 review summarises health-beneficial properties of oats.[9]

Rice is a staple for over half of the world's population; cooked white rice is mostly water with about 29% carbohydrate, about 2% protein and little fat, roughly 130 kcal per 100 g, and it is described as a protein source that is not complete on its own because it lacks sufficient amounts of some essential amino acids.[4] Wikipedia notes that brown rice has only the husk removed, while further milling removes the bran and germ to give white rice.[4]

Chicken is the second most consumed meat in the world after pork, and became more common in the United States during World War II when beef and pork were scarce.[5] Wikipedia gives the safe minimum cooking temperature for chicken as 165 degrees Fahrenheit (74 degrees Celsius) and notes that raw chicken may contain Salmonella.[5]

Wikipedia's article on muscle hypertrophy states that over the long term a positive energy balance supports anabolism and hence growth, that mechanical tension from resistance training is the currently accepted driver of the stimulus, and that protein intakes up to about 1.6 g per kilogram of body weight per day help increase strength and muscle size with training.[2] It cites evidence that intakes above about 1.8 g per kilogram showed no extra hypertrophy benefit, while noting that bodybuilders often recommend 2 to 4 g per kilogram and that one author recommends at least 2.2 g per kilogram for intense athletes.[2] The bodybuilding article likewise reports that views range from about 1 g per pound of body weight to 1.5, 2 or more.[1]

Carbohydrates are described as the main fuel for training and recovery, and bodybuilders typically prefer slowly digested sources, with faster sugars such as dextrose or maltodextrin used around workouts to replenish glycogen.[1] A 2023 narrative review of food-first carbohydrate strategies for athletes lists oats and rice among mixed carbohydrate foods that are effective pre-exercise sources, while cautioning about gastrointestinal comfort and palatability when large quantities are needed.[10]

On meal frequency, some bodybuilders eat five to seven meals every two to three hours, which can make large food volumes easier to eat during a bulk; controlled studies using calorimetry found no metabolic advantage to eating more often than three times a day.[1]

Within the clean-bulk framework, people alternate higher-calorie and lower-calorie days, or keep a small steady surplus to limit fat gain.[1] The 'standard bulk' name is used for the plain approach of simply eating more of ordinary foods, while 'dirty bulk' and 'lean bulk' describe the sloppier and more controlled ends of the spectrum.[1] Oat flour is sometimes made at home by pulsing rolled oats and added to shakes or baking as a way to raise calories without volume.[3]

Protein recommendations vary among experts, with some favouring about 1 g per pound of body weight and others more or less.[1] Wikipedia also states that bodybuilding authorities are unsure whether enough lean mass can be kept during cutting for the full cycle to be worthwhile.[1]

Randomised trials of oats against rice have been done in other contexts: a 2021 trial gave 210 mildly hypercholesterolaemic adults 80 g of oats or rice daily for 45 days and examined blood lipids and gut microbiota, and a 2025 trial compared low-gluten diets rich in oats or rice over 6 weeks in metabolically challenged volunteers.[6][7] These studies were not about muscle gain.

Forum posters describe eating large quantities of oats as part of weight-gain efforts, with one looksmax.org thread author saying they hoped it would have some positive effect.[8] Hacker News discussions in 2024 covered media stories on oats and weight management, which concern weight loss rather than bulking.[11][11] In looksmaxxing's framing, gaining muscle through a bulk is part of the body-composition side of improving appearance, alongside later cutting to reveal it.[1]

Larger surpluses and longer bulks add more body fat, which some lifters report needing a harder cut afterward.[1] Heavy intake of processed, sugary or high-fat foods in dirty bulking has been linked by Wikipedia to cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity concerns over time.[1] Oats contain avenins and can be cross-contaminated with wheat, so people with coeliac disease need caution.[3] Raw chicken may carry Salmonella, and Wikipedia reports surveys finding antibiotic-resistant bacteria on retail poultry.[5]
No studies found on oats, rice and chicken as a specific bulking diet. Related trials compared oats with rice for cholesterol and gut-health outcomes.[6][7]

lore.intro: Cheap staples such as oats, rice and chicken are a recurring theme in lifting and looksmaxxing talk about gaining weight on a budget.

claims.claim: Oats and rice are an efficient way to reach a calorie surplus.
Oats mimic weight-loss drugs, so they are a poor choice for bulking.
A clean bulk gains muscle with little fat.
More protein is always better for muscle gain.
Eating five to seven small meals speeds metabolism.

A study sparks the late-1980s US oat bran fad, which faded by 1990.[3]
